/japan/kanto/tokyo/imperial-palace-east-: The inner compounds of Edo Castle, from which the Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan, open as a public garden beside the Imperial Palace since 1968.

This is the ground of the shoguns’ government: the base of the tallest keep ever built in Japan, guardhouses that still stand, and the site of the corridor where the story of the forty-seven rōnin began.
Photo by Kuniteru I (active about 1818–1860), Public domain.
Photo by Guilhem Vellut from Annecy, France, CC BY 2.0.

The gardens are laid out on parts of three compounds of Edo Castle, the Honmaru, Ninomaru and Sannomaru, kept as a garden attached to the Imperial Palace and opened to the public in 1968. From here, from 1603, the Tokugawa shoguns governed Japan for nearly 260 years.

The way in is still through their gates. Ōtemon, the castle’s main gate, used by the shogun and the lords, is two gates set at right angles so that attackers would be trapped between them; its larger gate burned in an air raid and was rebuilt in 1967.[1][4][5]
Photograph: A moat of Edo Castle with a corner of dressed stone wall and pines above it.

Edo Castle’s keep was the tallest ever built in Japan. After the great fire of 1657 destroyed the third tower to stand here, the fourth shogun, Ietsuna, began a replacement at once and had the stone base finished by 1658: 46 metres by 42, ten metres high.
The tower itself was never built. Ietsuna’s uncle pointed out that a country at peace no longer needed such an enormous show of strength, and the base has stood empty ever since.[2]
Photograph: Looking out over the Honmaru lawn from the base of the vanished keep.
Guards, a turret, and the forty-seven rōnin

The Hyakunin Bansho, the hundred-man guardhouse, 45 metres long, controlled the way into the main compound: it was manned day and night by four shifts of a hundred samurai. With the keep gone, the Fujimi Yagura, sixteen metres tall on a fifteen-metre rampart, became the castle’s symbol.

Inside the main compound a corridor about 55 metres long, painted with pines, linked the shogun’s reception rooms. In it, in 1701, Lord Asano of Akō drew his sword on the court official Kira. Asano was ordered to take his own life, and a year later forty-seven of his retainers killed Kira in revenge, the story the theatre calls Chūshingura.[6][3][7]
Photograph: A woodblock print of the Chūshingura story: in a palace corridor, one lord lunges with a sword at another as attendants rush in.

Between 1983 and 1985 Emperor Shōwa had a wood made in the Ninomaru to stand for the Musashino woodland west of Tokyo, then disappearing under suburbs. Soil was brought from land about to be built on, and the seeds, roots and insect eggs in it grew back into the old woodland on their own.[8]
Photograph: Red maples and clipped azaleas in the Ninomaru garden in autumn, visitors on the paths.

/japan/kanto/tokyo/shibuya/: The district around the crossing that has become a picture of Tokyo: a wave of people across it every two minutes, a statue of a faithful dog beside it, and streets that set fashion.
Photo by Dick Thomas Johnson from Tokyo, Japan, CC BY 2.0.

More foreign visitors to Tokyo go to Shibuya than anywhere else in the city: six in ten in 2025, first for four years running. Its crossing has become the picture of modern Tokyo, and its best-loved landmark is a dog who waited there for ten years.
60.3%, first of any area for the fourth year running[1]As of 2025
Unveiled 21 April 1934, rebuilt after the war[3]
Photo by Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert, CC BY-SA 4.0.

When the lights change outside Shibuya Station, every direction walks at once. Tokyo's own travel guide counts upwards of a thousand people crossing the many-cornered intersection at a time, a wave that floods it every two minutes, and somehow nobody collides.

Photographs of it run in fashion and travel magazines around the world, and it has become a picture of the city itself. To see the pattern of it, look down from the cafés and station buildings around it.[2][4]
Photograph: A rainy day at the crossing, people under clear and coloured umbrellas crossing towards the station square.

Hachi, an Akita dog born in Ōdate in November 1923, belonged to Ueno Hidesaburō, a professor of agriculture at Tokyo Imperial University. He walked his master to Shibuya Station in the mornings and waited there for him in the evenings. On 21 May 1925 Ueno died suddenly at work, and did not come back.

Hachi went on waiting, outside the ticket gates morning and evening, in rain and snow. A newspaper article in 1932 made him famous, and in 1934 a bronze statue of him went up outside the station; he was at the unveiling. He died on 8 March 1935, aged 13, after almost ten years, and was buried beside his master in Aoyama Cemetery.
The statue was melted down for the war effort in 1944 and rebuilt three years after the war ended. It is now the most popular meeting place in Japan.[3]
Photograph: The bronze statue of Hachikō, an Akita dog sitting upright on a stone plinth, outside Shibuya Station.

Tokyo's guide calls Shibuya the city's trend-setting powerhouse for fashion. The round tower of Shibuya109 is a mecca for fashion-conscious teenagers, Hikarie and Parco are newer complexes for more polished shopping and dining, and the lanes of Jinnan are full of independent select shops.

The district keeps adding to itself. At MIYASHITA PARK you can eat local food from all over Japan, and in Shibuya Yokocho small restaurants serve everything from sushi and ramen to meals cooked by former sumo wrestlers.[4]
Photograph: Shibuya at night: buildings stacked with lit signs and screens over the crossing.

Each year the Tokyo government asks foreign visitors where they went. In 2025, 60.3% had been to Shibuya, ahead of Ginza (54.1%) and the area around Tokyo Station (51.8%), and Shibuya has led the list every year since 2022. Visitors from nineteen of the twenty countries and regions surveyed put it in their top three.[1]
Photograph: People waiting and resting on the benches of the square around the Hachikō statue, trees above.

/japan/kanto/nikko/nikko-toshogu/: The shrine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the first Tokugawa shogun, rebuilt by his grandson in 1636 as 55 buildings of lacquer, colour and carving.

Ieyasu laid the ground for some 260 years of peace, and his grandson spent a fortune on his shrine: one gate alone carries more than five hundred carvings, each meant to be read. It has been World Heritage since 1999.
55, eight of them National Treasures[2][3]
Photo by Mauricio V. Genta, CC BY-SA 4.0.
Photo by Maarten Heerlien from Voorschoten, The Netherlands, CC BY 2.0.

Tokugawa Ieyasu was born in 1542 at Okazaki Castle, ended the age of civil war and set up the government that would rule for the next 260 years. He died at Sunpu Castle in 1616, aged 75, and was buried at Kunōzan. By his own instructions he was moved here a year later and enshrined on 17 April 1617. In 1645 the shrine was given the title Tōshōgū.[1]
Photograph: A torii and the pagoda glimpsed through cedar branches on the way in.

Twenty years after the enshrinement, the third shogun, Iemitsu, Ieyasu’s grandson, rebuilt the shrine. Fifty-five buildings went up in a year and five months, at a recorded cost of 568,000 ryō of gold, 100 kan of silver and 1,000 koku of rice. They follow the slope of the mountain, linked by paths and stairs, and their lacquer, colour and carvings carry ideas from belief and learning, not just decoration.[1][2]
Photograph: The red five-storey pagoda in the shrine grounds, its eaves painted in green and gold.

Yōmeimon carries more than five hundred carved figures: Chinese sages, scenes from the classics, children at play, real and imagined animals. It is called the Higurashimon, the gate you could look at all day without tiring.

One of its twelve pillars is carved upside down. It is said that the moment something becomes perfect it begins to decline, and the flaw was likely meant to keep the shrine, and the Tokugawa, from declining. Beyond it, the Karamon is painted white with gofun, ground from seashells, then rare and costly, and was opened only for dignitaries.[4][5]
Photograph: The front of Yōmeimon, white carved beasts along its beam and gold and colour packed into every bracket above.

In Japanese lore monkeys protect horses, so eight carved panels of monkeys line the sacred stable, following a life from birth onward. The second is the famous one: see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.

Over the corridor to the inner shrine sleeps a small carved cat, attributed to Hidari Jingorō, and on a storehouse a carved elephant, drawn by Kanō Tan’yū, is one the artist could only imagine.[6][2][5][3]
Photograph: The carved monkeys of the sacred stable: one covers its ears, one its mouth, among painted pine branches.

/japan/kanto/kamakura/kotoku-in/: The temple of the Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze Amida more than eleven metres tall that has sat in the open air since its hall was lost.
Photo by Maarten Heerlien from Voorschoten, The Netherlands, CC BY 2.0.
Smaller than Nara’s Great Buddha but much closer to its original form, it is a National Treasure and a model of Kamakura-period sculpture. Nobody knows who made it.
Photo by Dick Thomas Johnson from Tokyo, Japan, CC BY 2.0.
Photo by Gilles Desjardins, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Azumakagami, the chronicle of the Kamakura shogunate, says work on the Great Buddha began in 1252, and the priest Jōkō is believed to have collected the donations that paid for it. Much else is unclear, including who made it. Its style shows the influence of the Kei school of sculptors and of Song-dynasty China, and it is taken as a typical work of Kamakura-period sculpture.

It is Amida, the Buddha of the Western Pure Land, and the temple belongs to the Jōdo sect founded by Hōnen, which teaches that calling Amida’s name, Namu Amida Butsu, is enough to be reborn in his Pure Land.[1][2]
Photograph: The Buddha's face close up: half-closed eyes, a straight nose and the seams of the casting across the bronze.

The statue was first housed in a hall. Records say storms damaged and destroyed it in 1334 and 1369, and an earthquake in 1498 finished it; the Japan Tourism Agency’s text says it was a tsunami that took the last hall. Since then the Buddha has sat in the open, which makes it unusual among Japan’s great Buddhas.
In the middle of the Edo period the priests Yūten and Yokoku repaired it with money from Nojima Shinzaemon, a merchant of Asakusa, and restored the temple as Kōtoku-in Shōjōsen-ji.[1][3]
Photograph: The Great Buddha seen from the side across the temple grounds, trees and hills behind.

The figure was cast from the bottom up between an outer and an inner mould, with earth piled around them for support as each stage was poured; the body alone took seven large stages. From inside you can see it is made of some forty separately cast sections, joined in three different ways.
It was once covered in gold leaf. Traces can still be seen on the right cheek.[4][5][6]
Photograph: Inside the hollow statue, looking up at the joined bronze sections and rows of hair curls cast from within.

The temple sets its figures beside those of Tōdai-ji’s Great Buddha in Nara: 11.3 metres tall against nearly 15, 121 tonnes against 250. Kamakura’s has more hair curls, 656 against 492, and nearly as wide an eye.[2]
Photograph: The Niō Gate at the entrance to Kōtoku-in, a red-pillared gate with a green copper roof and a plaque above the opening.
